questions.prompt: You have fifteen minutes and no AI experience. What fits this episode?
options: Try a small task whose result you can judge.
Finish a technical course before opening a tool.
Hand over a high-stakes decision to save time.
Find the best model for every possible task.
questions.explain: Start with a bounded, low-risk task. You can learn from the result without solving every AI question first.
optionFeedback: A familiar task gives you a way to judge the draft, even on your first try.
You can learn by trying one manageable task; a technical course is not a prerequisite.
Start where a mistake is easy to catch and repair. A consequential decision needs more than a quick first try.
You only need a useful tool for this task. One attempt cannot settle every future choice.

questions.prompt: You want to try the invitation exercise in a personal AI tool. Which input fits?
options: A copied conversation with everyone’s private details.
An invented situation with the choices the message needs.
A client email with only the client’s name removed.
A colleague’s document because it is on your laptop.
questions.explain: An invented situation lets you practise without sharing someone else’s private information. Access to a document is not permission to upload it.
optionFeedback: The other people’s private details are unnecessary for this practice. Invent the situation instead.
You keep the useful constraints while leaving real people’s private information out.
Names are not the only identifying or sensitive details. An invented example avoids relying on name removal.
Being able to open a document does not establish permission to share it with an AI provider.

questions.prompt: The product writes an invitation you have never seen before. What is it doing?
options: Finding a verified invitation that matches your life.
Retraining its entire model on your short request.
Generating content from learned patterns and available context.
Confirming that every proposed detail is correct.
questions.explain: It is generating a draft. Producing new wording does not establish that the facts or suggestions in it are right.
optionFeedback: A generated invitation is not a verified record of your plans. Check the details against what you actually supplied.
This reply uses the model’s learned patterns; your request supplies context for the answer.
The product uses learned patterns and available context to produce the wording. You still check what that wording claims.
Producing a sentence and checking its truth are different jobs. A draft can propose something nobody arranged.

questions.prompt: Two products give different drafts for the same request. What can you conclude?
options: The more polished product must have the better model.
The shorter draft proves the product ignored your request.
A model and a product are two names for the same thing.
Models, context, settings and features can affect the result.
questions.explain: You are comparing product experiences. The model matters, but the instructions, available context and surrounding features can also differ.
optionFeedback: Polish tells you about this draft’s presentation. It does not establish which underlying model is better.
A short draft may fit the request. Check whether it includes what you needed before judging it by length.
The model is a trained component; the product includes the features and instructions around it.
Several parts of the product experience can change the answer, even when you type the same request.

questions.prompt: The invitation includes the right days but says a table is booked. Nobody booked it. What matters?
options: The whole answer is useless because one detail is wrong.
It contains an unsupported detail inside useful wording.
A polished draft means the restaurant was verified.
The restaurant is safe to keep because it is plausible.
questions.explain: The reservation is made up. Keep any useful wording, but remove the false claim before using the invitation.
optionFeedback: One false detail needs correction, but the surrounding wording may still be useful. Check and edit the draft.
You spotted the false reservation without treating every sentence as worthless. Remove that claim before sending.
A finished-looking invitation is not evidence of a booking. Check what has actually been arranged.
A believable restaurant plan is still false if nobody made it. Plausibility cannot supply the missing booking.

questions.prompt: Your draft is far too formal. Which next move could help?
options: Explain the audience and tone, then review the revision.
Ask it to sound more confident about the same wording.
Assume it knows your friends from your account name.
Switch products without saying what needs to change.
questions.explain: Relevant context can help shape a better draft. It still needs your review; the instruction does not guarantee a perfect result.
optionFeedback: Audience and tone give the revision a clearer target. Your next job is to check whether it fits.
More confidence would not fix the formal tone. Describe how the invitation should sound to its recipients.
An account name does not tell the product how you and your friends speak to each other. Supply the relevant context.
Another product might write differently, but it still needs to know what you want changed.

questions.prompt: Why keep the request the same when comparing products?
options: To prove which model will be best for the whole season.
To make every product return identical sentences.
To make differences in their responses easier to notice.
To avoid having to check any of the finished drafts.
questions.explain: Changing both the request and the product makes the comparison harder to interpret. This is a useful look at these results, not a permanent ranking.
optionFeedback: This comparison concerns these responses to this task. Different tasks or later product changes can give different results.
The same request can still produce different wording. Those differences are what you are examining.
Keeping the request steady makes the response differences easier to inspect.
A comparison is not a fact-check. Each draft still needs checking against your actual task.

questions.prompt: A survey finds that women use AI less often on average. What does that measure?
options: How capable women are of learning to use AI.
How accurate every woman’s AI-assisted work is.
How much each individual woman should use AI.
A difference in reported participation between groups.
questions.explain: Use and ability are different measures. An average across groups also cannot describe every woman or every workplace.
optionFeedback: The survey measured use. It did not test women’s ability to learn the tools.
How often people use AI does not tell you whether their resulting work is accurate.
A group average is not a prescription for one person. Your useful level of use depends on your tasks and circumstances.
Reported participation describes use across groups; it does not assign an ability level to individuals.

questions.prompt: The draft follows your instructions but would upset the person receiving it. What now?
options: Send it because following the prompt is the standard.
Revise it using what you know about the situation.
Treat the tool’s certainty as better social judgment.
Assume another generated draft needs no review.
questions.explain: Your knowledge of the relationship matters. A draft can follow instructions and still be wrong for the real situation.
optionFeedback: Following the words of a request is not enough if the result damages the relationship. Check the likely effect.
You know something the draft missed. Use that knowledge to make the message fit its real recipient.
A certain tone is not evidence that the product understands this relationship.
Another draft may help, but you still need to check how it would land with this person.

questions.prompt: You can only access one of the three products today. What should you do?
options: Try the task there and save what you learn.
Wait until you can pay for all three products.
Use confidential work material to make it worthwhile.
Skip review because there is nothing to compare it with.
questions.explain: You can get a useful first result with one product. Review it against your task and add a comparison later if you want.
optionFeedback: One tool is enough for a first attempt you can judge. You can keep that work and compare later.
Three subscriptions are not required for a useful first try. Start with what you can access.
Confidential material does not make practice more valuable. Use a permitted task or invented details.
You can check a draft against your needs and facts without having a second AI answer beside it.

questions.prompt: Does typing your request automatically retrain the model for this answer?
options: Yes; each message rebuilds the model before it replies.
Yes; only paid accounts use previously trained models.
No; the request supplies context for this answer.
No; the product cannot use the request at all.
questions.explain: Your message supplies current context. Whether a provider later uses conversations to improve systems is a separate question that depends on its product and settings.
optionFeedback: Supplying a message as context is different from rebuilding the trained model.
A paid plan does not make each request a new training run. Payment and this distinction are separate questions.
The request helps shape this answer. Possible later use of conversations for training is a separate question.
The request is usable context. Not retraining on it does not mean the product ignores it.

questions.prompt: What does David Rose help us practise next episode?
options: Trusting the draft with the most confident tone.
Saying exactly what result, audience and constraints matter.
Choosing a permanent winner among all AI products.
Adding more references instead of clarifying the request.
questions.explain: Specificity: tell it what you want and what would make the result useful. The next episode develops that skill.
optionFeedback: Confidence is part of how an answer sounds; David’s lesson is about making the request specific.
Result, audience and constraints make “what I want” clear enough to act on.
David’s lesson helps you brief a task; it does not establish one product as a permanent winner.
A reference helps only if it clarifies the job. More references cannot replace saying what result you need.
